evidence.reason: Sink: attacker-controlled directory/filename (argv[1]/argv[2], line 58) flow through filepath (line 23) into an open that truncates any pre-existing inode and follows symlinks; with no O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW equivalent, an attacker who can place a 0644 file or a symlink at that path in a shared directory gets the secret written there with pre-existing permissions or at the link destination.

evidence.snippet: mode_t oldUmask = umask(0077); // Owner can read and write only
evidence.reason: Root cause of the permission failure: umask is applied only when open(2) creates a new file; it retroactively cannot fix an existing file's mode bits and does not block symlink resolution, so the 0600 guarantee at line 9 relies on an unverified assumption that the target does not already exist.

assumptions: The threat model includes another unprivileged user who can create files/symlinks in the target directory (e.g., a shared directory such as /tmp); the shown code imposes no restriction on directory.
std::ofstream(out|trunc) compiles to open(2) with O_CREAT|O_TRUNC and mode 0666&~umask, following symlinks and reusing existing inodes; pre-existing files keep their mode bits.
limitations: Path traversal via filename containing '/' or '..' is not reported as a vulnerability: directory and filename both come from argv at the same trust level (line 58), so no privilege boundary is crossed in the shown code; it would become exploitable only if directory were trusted and filename were not.
umask is not restored if an exception unwinds the function before lines 32/40/46 (e.g., std::bad_alloc); no concrete attacker trigger exists in this single-threaded entry point.
umask is process-global state; an embedder using threads could observe a restricted umask in other threads, but no such concurrency exists in the shown main().

The attack requires the target path to already exist with loose permissions or as a symlink before the open; this filesystem-state precondition cannot be satisfied by the shown code alone, but is the standard CWE-377/CWE-59 scenario for predictable-name secret files.

verdict.summary: The directory-boundary check compares only the directory prefix without requiring a '/' or NUL boundary, so sibling directories sharing the prefix are accepted and their files read; the realpath validation is TOCTOU with the later fopen on the original path; and realpath writes into fixed 1024-byte stack buffers without PATH_MAX-size enforcement, allowing attacker-controlled paths/symlinks to overflow the stack.

evidence.reason: The guard compares only strlen(dir_realpath) bytes and never checks that the next byte is '/' or NUL. With dir_path resolving to /var/www/app and filename ../app-secret/flag, file_realpath becomes /var/www/app-secret/flag, strncmp over 12 bytes returns 0, the return at line 38 is skipped, and fopen at line 42 reads a file outside the intended directory. Taint originates at argv[1] (line 74) and flows unvalidated through lines 27 and 31 to line 42.

file_path was validated by realpath at line 31 and by the prefix check at line 36, but fopen at line 42 re-resolves the same attacker-influenced path from scratch, following any symlink inserted or swapped between the check and the open. An attacker able to replace the validated entry with a symlink to a sensitive file during that window bypasses the boundary check. This is a time-of-check/time-of-use race (CWE-367) on the attacker-controlled filename/dir_path from argv.

file_realpath is declared as char[1024] at line 30, but realpath requires a buffer of at least PATH_MAX bytes and has no length parameter. On systems where PATH_MAX exceeds 1024, an attacker-controlled short file_path containing a symlink with a long target, or a long dir_path, resolves to an absolute path longer than 1024 bytes, so realpath writes past the stack buffer. The same unbounded write exists for dir_realpath at line 21. CWE-121.

assumptions: The intended trust boundary is that dir_path is a server-chosen root and only filename is attacker-controlled; if dir_path itself is fully attacker-controlled, the prefix restriction is moot but still bypassable.
argv strings are NUL-terminated and cannot contain embedded NUL bytes.
realpath assumes a PATH_MAX-sized output buffer and PATH_MAX may exceed 1024 on the target platform.
For the TOCTOU and symlink-expansion cases, the attacker can modify filesystem entries (create/rename symlinks) in the affected directories.
limitations: The realpath overflow depends on PATH_MAX > 1024 and libc behavior; on platforms with PATH_MAX <= 1024 it reduces to realpath returning NULL rather than a stack overflow.
The TOCTOU requires a concurrent filesystem write during the check-to-use window at lines 31/36 to 42.
Unchecked realloc at lines 52 and 60 can NULL-dereference on allocation failure; recorded as a robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.
Reading the entire file with no size limit can exhaust memory (CWE-400); impact is DoS and was not counted as a confirmed finding.
char ch in the fgetc loop treats byte 0xFF as EOF on signed-char platforms and printf stops at the first NUL, so binary content is truncated; correctness-only, no memory safety impact.
content_size + 1 overflow in the read loop is theoretical on 32-bit systems for files near SIZE_MAX and was not counted as a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The subdomain prefix is validated with the anchored character-class regex ^[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+$ before being concatenated into the URL, which excludes every host-injection delimiter (@, /, ?, #, :, whitespace). The resulting host is always <subdomain_pref>.domain under https://, so no authority/path/open-redirect injection is reachable. No memory-safety or ReDoS issues exist: argv is guarded by the argc check and the regex is linear.

evidence.reason: This validation is the only guard controlling the attacker-controlled subdomain_prefix (from argv[2], line 40). It restricts the entire input to ASCII letters, digits, dot, and dash, which is the full character set used in the later concatenation at line 26.

Any input reaching the URL-construction sink must pass the regex, so the host component can only be <subdomain_prefix>.<domain> under the trusted domain. Characters required to escape the authority (@, /, ?, #, :, whitespace) are excluded, so no concrete attacker value can alter the host, path, or protocol at the sink (line 26). Injection reachability fails.

assumptions: domain is trusted per the documented contract and not attacker-controlled; the code intentionally does not validate it.
The returned string is only printed to stdout in the shown code; any downstream fetch/redirect behavior is outside the shown code.
limitations: If a downstream consumer later treats the returned string as a URL and fetches it, that behavior is not shown here; however, even then the allowed character set prevents escaping the trusted domain's host.

Inputs with leading/trailing dots or dashes (e.g., "-" or ".")) pass the regex but produce non-RFC hostnames (e.g., "https://-.example.com"), a correctness/robustness concern without a confirmed security impact.

The trusted domain itself receives no validation; if that invariant is violated by a future caller, injective content in the domain could propagate into the URL, but no such path exists in the shown code.

verdict.summary: vp8_decoder_remove_threads is a defensive teardown routine. Re-entry is prevented by the b_multithreaded_rd guard (set false before cleanup) and both loops are bounded by allocated_decoding_thread_count with no off-by-one in the loop logic. No attacker-controlled input reaches this function in the shown code, and all potential issues (array bounds, NULL array state, worker-thread synchronization/use-after-destroy) depend on allocation and thread-lifecycle invariants defined outside the shown code, so none can be confirmed as a reachable vulnerability.

evidence.reason: The guard at line 2 and the early clear at line 4 make the teardown non-re-entrant, preventing double-free/double-join on repeated calls. The loop bound at line 6 limits i to allocated_decoding_thread_count-1 with no off-by-one, so no OOB is reachable from the loop logic itself; safety of the indices against the true array capacities is an invariant enforced only at the unshown allocation site.

assumptions: pbi is a caller-provided decoder context whose array/thread fields are consistent with allocated_decoding_thread_count; that consistency is established by code outside this function.
vpx_free(NULL) is safe, so the NULL-assignment after each free in lines 15-24 is defensive.
limitations: Out-of-bounds access at lines 7, 8, 12 would require allocated_decoding_thread_count to exceed the true allocated size of h_event_start_decoding/h_decoding_thread; sizes are not declared or verified in the shown code, so this is an unconfirmed robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.
NULL dereference at lines 7, 8, 12 if an array is NULL while the count is nonzero depends on allocation failure or a caller violating the allocation invariant; out of scope per the rules.
Potential use-after-free / use-after-destroy of h_event_end_decoding (line 14) or worker thread state depends on the unshown worker-loop synchronization state, so it cannot be confirmed.
Integer overflow of the int loop counter i would require allocated_decoding_thread_count > INT_MAX, which is not derivable from any shown input; theoretical only.
Behavior of the helper vp8mt_de_alloc_temp_buffers (line 26) is not shown and is not analyzed.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability: all writes into the 256-byte static url buffer (line 20) go through snprintf with an explicit size cap MAX_URL_LENGTH (lines 24, 27, 29), so unbounded attacker-controlled argv[1]/argv[2] strings cannot overflow it, and the format strings are literals. Residual issues (silent truncation, no subdomain character validation, shared static buffer) are robustness/spec concerns with no security impact inside the shown main() code.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled argv[1]/argv[2] flow unvalidated into the %s arguments, but snprintf's size argument MAX_URL_LENGTH (256) bounds the write to at most 255 chars plus NUL, exactly the size of url declared at line 20; no input length can exceed the buffer, and user data is never interpreted as a format string.

The only input-dependent guard. Both outcomes (line 27 and line 29) remain bounded by snprintf, so the guard's narrowness affects only URL well-formedness (e.g., allowing '/', '#', '@'), not memory safety; any open-redirect/SSRF impact would require an out-of-scope consumer of the returned string.

assumptions: argv strings are NUL-terminated with no embedded NULs, per the C/C++ runtime contract.
std::string::c_str() returns a NUL-terminated buffer (C++11+ standard guarantee).
main() is the only caller and runs single-threaded, so the static url buffer is not accessed concurrently.
snprintf succeeds (no output error), so it always NUL-terminates within the 256-byte buffer.
limitations: Silent truncation: inputs whose concatenated URL exceeds 255 chars are truncated because snprintf's return value is ignored (lines 27, 29); the resulting URL can be malformed (e.g., a cut-down host). This is a robustness concern only, and in the shown code the string is merely printed at line 47.

Subdomain validation is missing (line 26 checks length only); a prefix such as 'attacker.com/' or 'attacker.com#' yields a URL whose parsed host is not under the trusted domain. Impact (open redirect/SSRF/URL confusion) is unconfirmed because the shown code only prints the URL and never navigates/fetches it.

The static url buffer (line 20) makes get_url_to_visit non-reentrant and racy under concurrent calls; this is unreachable from the shown single-threaded main() and is a hardening concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled 32-bit len (ntohl of the RPC payload) flows into XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4. For len in {0xFFFFFFFD..0xFFFFFFFF}, len+3 wraps to zero, making XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4 == 0 and bypassing the dlen data-length guard at line 39. len is then clamped to max_blocksize while actual received page data is small, so the unbounded while loop (lines 49-54) writes rq_vec[v]/reads rq_pages[v] past the end of the framework arrays, yielding an out-of-bounds read/write and kernel memory corruption.

evidence.reason: len (line 16) is attacker-controlled 32-bit unsigned. XDR_QUADLEN(len) is ((len+3)>>2); for len = 0xFFFFFFFD, len+3 wraps to 0, so XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4 = 0 and 'dlen < 0' is always false, bypassing the guard that otherwise requires actual received data >= len.

With the line 39 guard bypassed, len is clamped to max_blocksize (line 44) but the actual received page data is small. The loop has no bound on v against the rq_vec/rq_pages array sizes, so it writes rq_vec[v] and reads rq_pages[v] out of bounds, driven by the inflated len.

assumptions: XDR_QUADLEN(l) is defined as ((l) + 3) >> 2 on a 32-bit unsigned int, so len+3 can wrap modulo 2^32.
len is unsigned int (32-bit), so the overflow at line 39 is well-defined.
limitations: The exact out-of-bounds extent in the loop depends on RPCSVC_MAXPAGES (size of rq_vec/rq_pages) and on svc_max_payload(rqstp), which are defined in headers not shown here.

The plain loop overflow (without the XDR_QUADLEN bypass) is mitigated by the max_blocksize clamp at lines 42-45; the residual confirmed defect is the integer overflow at line 39 that defeats the dlen check.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled pts_inc from the container header reaches signed arithmetic and a rational reducer without validation. A crafted value such as 0x40000000 overflows at pts_inc *= 100 (wrapping to 0), and a value of 0 yields the same zero denominator; the zero is then passed to av_reduce, producing undefined behavior and a likely divide-by-zero crash, while the signed overflow is itself UB.

evidence.reason: Taint source: the 32-bit file value is cast to int32_t without validation; an attacker sets it to 0x40000000 (or 0) to trigger the failure.

Reachable sink: 0x40000000 is not negative, so line 61 performs the signed overflow 0x40000000*100 which wraps to 0; value 0 also stays 0. Line 63 then passes the resulting zero as av_reduce's denominator, whose gcd/arithmetic divides by it, crashing via division-by-zero; even without the callee, line 61 is signed-overflow UB.

assumptions: SmackerContext's frames and treesize fields are 32-bit unsigned, consistent with get_le32 assignment, so frames*4 and treesize+16 are covered by the existing checks.
av_reduce performs integer division on its denominator (through av_gcd) and is not tolerant of a zero denominator.
limitations: The divide-by-zero impact depends on the unshown av_reduce/av_gcd implementation; if that library code rejects zero denominators, the residual impact is signed-overflow UB and an incorrect time base.
Unchecked av_malloc of frm_size/frm_flags (lines 36-37) dereferenced at lines 41/44 can null-deref, but only on allocation failure; recorded as a robustness concern.
ast[i] from av_new_stream (line 69) is dereferenced at line 70 without a null check, but only an allocation failure reaches it.
Unvalidated width/height (lines 51-52) may affect downstream decoding, but no dangerous sink for them is present in the shown code.
Negation of INT32_MIN at line 59 is an additional signed-overflow UB site, not confirmed as an independent vulnerability.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in the shown code. The whitespace skip (lines 16-17) is bounded by the NUL terminator proven by strchr; the memmove (line 26) copies a suffix of maddr->user back onto itself (size strlen(p)+1 fits within the array); and the only copy into maddr->domain uses strlcpy with sizeof(maddr->domain) (lines 41-42). Any overflow would have to occur inside the not-shown text_to_mailaddr/valid_* callees, which is out of scope and recorded as a limitation.

evidence.reason: e points at line[k] where line[k] == '>' and k < strlen(line) (strchr at line 12); after *e++ = '\0', e = &line[k+1], and k+1 <= strlen(line), so every byte read by the loop is within the NUL-terminated line, stopping at the terminator. No read can pass line[strlen(line)].

p is a pointer into maddr->user (strchr), so strlen(p)+1 is exactly the live suffix [p..NUL] of the same array; memmove copies it to user[0]. Source and destination are both within user[] (overlap is legal for memmove), so no OOB read or write is reachable regardless of the attacker-controlled address content.
The only write into maddr->domain in the shown code is bounded by sizeof(maddr->domain), the true in-struct array size, so the trusted domain string is truncated safely and cannot overflow.

assumptions: line is NUL-terminated, as required by strchr at line 12 and strlen/memmove usage.
maddr->user and maddr->domain are in-struct arrays, making sizeof(maddr->domain) the array size (line 42).
maddr, args, and domain are non-NULL per caller contract; domain points to a valid C string.
The not-shown text_to_mailaddr (line 20) bounds-checks and NUL-terminates maddr->user/maddr->domain, keeping strchr/strlen on line 23-26 in bounds.
limitations: Any buffer overflow must originate in the not-shown text_to_mailaddr or valid_localpart/valid_domainpart; their code is absent, so no overflow can be tied to concrete lines here (unconfirmed hypothesis).
The sizes of maddr->user and maddr->domain are not shown, so exact capacity cannot be asserted; the shown memmove is safe for any size >= strlen(p)+1, which always holds since p is inside the array.

Historical context: this function shape is related to OpenSMTPD CVE-2020-7247, but the shown code contains the whitespace skip and strlcpy guards; the presence/absence of the actual vulnerable pattern cannot be verified without the full original version.
*args (line 18) points into the caller's line buffer; keeping that pointer valid after return is the caller's contract and is not verifiable from the shown code.
If a caller passed a non-NUL-terminated line or NULL domain (contract violations), strchr/strlcpy would be unsafe; those are out-of-scope caller errors, not reachable through the shown code alone.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in vp8_decoder_remove_threads. Both loops index h_event_start_decoding and h_decoding_thread with a strict i < allocated_decoding_thread_count bound (max index count-1), no off-by-one exists, the guard at line 4 plus the flag reset at line 8 prevent repeated teardown, and every freed pointer is set to NULL. All potential out-of-bounds or uninitialized-resource failures would require allocation/count invariants established outside the shown code and are recorded as limitations.

evidence.reason: This is the only branch in the function. It gates all teardown but performs no validation of allocated_decoding_thread_count, no NULL checks on h_event_start_decoding/h_decoding_thread, and no verification that the arrays were allocated with exactly count elements; every memory-safety property downstream therefore depends on invariants from the unseen thread-creation path.

Index i ranges over [0, count-1] due to the strict < comparison; the largest reachable index is count-1, so the accesses at lines 12-13 are in-bounds if and only if the (unseen) allocation matched the same count. No off-by-one exists in the shown loop, and count has no attacker-controlled source in this function, so the OOB hypothesis fails taint and reachability confirmation.

Same strict bound and index range as the first loop; every thread was joined at line 13 before these semaphores are destroyed, so no blocked thread races the destroy. The only failure mode (count exceeding allocation size) is not reachable from the shown code.

Every buffer is freed exactly once per entry and immediately set to NULL; combined with the flag reset at line 8 (which makes a second sequential call a no-op), there is no double-free or use-after-free path visible in the shown code.

assumptions: pbi->h_event_start_decoding and pbi->h_decoding_thread are allocated with exactly allocated_decoding_thread_count elements and fully initialized whenever b_multithreaded_rd is nonzero.
b_multithreaded_rd is set only after successful thread creation, so lines 12-13 never operate on NULL or uninitialized entries.
allocated_decoding_thread_count is non-negative, within INT_MAX, and not mutated concurrently with this function.
pbi->h_event_end_decoding was initialized with sem_init before line 19.
vpx_free(NULL) is safe (standard free semantics used by libvpx).
limitations: Heap out-of-bounds read/write on h_event_start_decoding/h_decoding_thread (lines 12-13, 17) is unconfirmed: it would require allocated_decoding_thread_count to exceed the actual allocation size, which can only be established in the unseen create-threads/init path (potential CWE-787/CWE-125).
pthread_join or sem_post on uninitialized/NULL entries (lines 12-13) would need b_multithreaded_rd set without successful allocation or thread creation; the shown code does not contain such a path.
No NULL dereference is confirmed: if the flag could be set while h_event_start_decoding is NULL, line 12 would fault, but that state depends on code not shown.
Concurrent invocation with the decode path (race on the shared VP8D_COMP state) is not analyzed because the shown code contains no locking; any such race is out of scope for this snippet.

verdict.summary: The secret file is created with effective mode 0644 instead of owner-only permissions because umask(0022) is combined with std::ofstream's default 0666 creation mode, making the file group/world-readable and violating the stated only-current-user requirement.

evidence.reason: std::ofstream creates a missing file with default mode 0666. With umask 0022 set at line 25, the resulting mode is 0666 & ~0022 = 0644, giving group and others read access. The secret is then written at line 36, and no chmod or explicit open mode restores owner-only permissions; line 16 only checks non-empty arguments, and the failure branches at lines 29-33/37-41 do not repair permissions.

assumptions: std::ofstream uses creation mode 0666 when creating a new file, subject to the process umask.
Other local users are treated as potential adversaries for the secret file; actual access also depends on the destination directory being traversable/readable, which the shown code never guarantees.
limitations: User-controlled filename/directory concatenated without normalization permits ../ and symlink-following writes outside the intended directory; this becomes a privilege-boundary violation only if the process runs with higher privileges than the invoking user or an external caller forces the victim to choose the adversarial path,neither of which is shown.
umask is a process-wide setting; concurrent threads creating files during the umask window could inherit the looser permissions, but the shown program is single-threaded at this call site.

Existing destination files are truncated without checking or correcting their current permission bits, so a pre-existing world-readable file remains world-readable; this shares the same root cause as the confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled RV10/RV20 header values mb_count/mb_x/mb_y are validated only with av_log() calls; no return or clamping occurs. The decode loop then iterates mb_count times and passes out-of-range s->mb_x/s->mb_y to ff_h263_decode_mb/MPV_decode_mb, causing an out-of-bounds write into per-macroblock picture/block storage.

evidence.reason: Both the position check and the count check only log errors; the attacker-controlled mb_count/mb_x/mb_y are not rejected or clamped, so mb_count and the resulting loop indices can exceed the frame's actual macroblock bounds.

The loop count is taken verbatim from whichever mb_count the header parser returned,with no clamp to left/remaining valid macroblocks; mb_count > left slips through the log-only guardat lines 20-22 and drives the loop past the frame boundary.

With mb_count = left+1, after the last valid row s->mb_y becomes equal to s->mb_height via the wrap at lines 83-86; this call then decodes/writes a macroblock at an out-of-range row, causing an out-of-bounds write in the per-macroblock decode path.

assumptions: The called per-MB functions ff_h263_decode_mb and MPV_decode_mb index internal picture/block storage by s->mb_x/s->mb_y; their bodies are outside this snippet, but this indexing contract is what makes an out-of-range MB position a memory-safety violation.
The header parser can return mb_count > left because the code explicitly anticipates that case with the COUNT ERROR check at line 20; otherwise that guard would be dead code.
limitations: The exact write overflow inside ff_h263_decode_mb/MPV_decode_mb is not shown here; if a nonexistent external implementation clamped those indices internally, the impact would not materialize, but no such clamp exists in the shown control flow.

The s->gb.size_in_bits =  ild.asignment at lines 70-73 could enlarge the logical bitstream capacity beyond the actual buf allocation if buf_size2 > buf_size, but the shown code does not establish the relationship between buf_size, buf_size2,and the allocation, so it is left as an unconfirmed robustness concern.
buf_size*8 at line  ild.can theoretically overflow an int, but demuxer packet-size limits likely constrain buf_size, so this is not reported as a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: decrypt_response indexes the input buffer in[0..4] (in[0] at line 16; in[1..4] in the cipher-length parsing at lines 20-31) before any validation of inlen. A card-supplied response shorter than the indexed offset causes an out-of-bounds read (info disclosure / crash). All other bounds (cipher_len, plaintext writes, unpadding index) are correctly guarded.

evidence.reason: in is attacker/device-controlled and its length inlen is never checked before this read; a response with inlen < 1 reads in[0] out of bounds (CWE-125). No prior `if (inlen < N)` guard exists in the shown code.

The cipher-length parse reads in[1], in[2], in[3], and in[4] before the only length check at line 37 (i+cipher_len > inlen). For a response with inlen < 5, the branch at line 28 reads in[4] out of bounds, confirming the missing inlen validation as the reachable OOB-read sink.

assumptions: card->drv_data is non-null and valid before the cast at line 13 (checked at line 10).
sizeof plaintext == 4096 as declared at line 7.
The CBC decrypt primitives write at most cipher_len-1 bytes to plaintext (standard CBC output length).
limitations: Reachability of the OOB read depends on a caller passing inlen < 5; if callers always guarantee inlen >= 5 the bug is latent (robustness concern).

The final memcpy(out, plaintext, cipher_len - 2) at line 53 writes cipher_len-2 bytes to out, but out's capacity is not validated here; an undersized out is a caller-contract issue, not confirmed within this function.
Impact magnitude (which and how many adjacent bytes are disclosed) depends on layout and the specific caller; exact disclosure not determinable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: On PLATFORM_WEB builds, SetClipboardText interpolates the caller-supplied text into a JavaScript snippet via TextFormat and executes it with emscripten_run_script without escaping. A single quote in the clipboard text breaks out of the JS string literal and executes arbitrary JavaScript in the page origin (e.g., text containing '); allows script injection).

evidence.reason: text (attacker-influenceable clipboard payload, Phase 1) is substituted verbatim into a single-quoted JS string literal by TextFormat and then executed by emscripten_run_script. No escaping or validation is applied, so a text value containing a single quote (e.g., '); closes the string literal early and the remainder executes as JavaScript in the page origin. This is reachable on any PLATFORM_WEB build where text contains a quote (Phase 3), confirming CWE-94 primary with CWE-79 secondary.

assumptions: The build in question defines PLATFORM_WEB, activating the vulnerable branch.
TextFormat behaves like a standard printf-style formatter that inserts the argument verbatim.
emscripten_run_script executes the supplied string as JavaScript in the page context.
limitations: The desktop branch (glfwSetClipboardString) is not vulnerable because it consumes text as data; no CWE is attributed to it.

Exploitation requires an attacker to influence the value passed as text (e.g., content copied into the clipboard), which depends on the out-of-scope caller and surrounding application; the injection mechanism itself is fully confirmed within the shown code.

verdict.summary: Missing bounds check on attacker-controlled ref_count[list] in ff_h264_pred_weight_table allows heap out-of-bounds writes to H264PredWeightTable.luma_weight/chroma_weight when picture_structure == PICT_FRAME and ref_count[list] > 16 (reachable with the decoder max of 32 from num_ref_idx_active).

evidence.reason: ref_count[list] is attacker-controlled (num_ref_idx_l0/l1_active_minus1, up to 32) and is used verbatim as loop bound with no check against the 48-element first dimension of pwt->luma_weight/chroma_weight, or against the ≤16 limit required by the PICT_FRAME mapping.

Under PICT_FRAME, the largest index written is 16+2*i+1 =  ️⃣15+2*ref_count[list] (i=ref_count[list]-1). With ref_count[list]=17, i=16 produces indices 48 and 49 individually, exceeding the last valid index 47 of the 48-element arrays; with ref_count up to 32, indices reach up to  ️⃣79. This is a reachable heap OOB write (CWE-787obtained.

assumptions: H264PredWeightTable is the standard FFmpeg struct with luma_weight[48][2][2], chroma_weight[48][2][2][2]; the 16+2*i frame mapping and 15+2*ref_count bound follow directly from that layout.
ref_count[list] is derived from the decoded num_ref_idx_l0/l1_active_minus1 fields, whose spec/decoder range is 0..32, making ref_count=17..32 reachable in practice.
limitations: The caller-side computation of ref_count is not shown in the snippet; if an external invariant clamped ref_count to ≤16 for frame pictures, this path would be unreachable — but no such clamp exists in the shown code,and the decoder's override path (num_ref_idx_active_override_flag) can yield ref_count up to 32.
The int8_t weight range checks (lines 32-33, 51-52) and denom clamps ( 13-20) are robustness guards only and do not mitigate the index overflow.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. The getter lookup is guarded by IsObject()/IsFunction() checks that fail-fast via RELEASE_NOTREACHED(), and the getter is invoked with argc=0/argv=0 (no user-controlled buffer, size, or index). fprintf uses literal format strings with trusted internal className/attributeName keys.

assumptions: className and attributeName are trusted, null-terminated const char* private-script keys supplied by internal Blink callers.
scriptState/scriptStateInUserScript are framework-internal execution contexts.
holder is the valid target DOM object established by the caller.
limitations: If a caller ever supplied a non-null-terminated className/attributeName, the fprintf %s at the shown lines could read out of bounds; this is not substantiated by the shown code (depends on an out-of-scope caller violating a string invariant).
Risks internal to unshown helpers (classObjectOfPrivateScript, initializeHolderIfNeeded, V8ScriptRunner::callFunction, rethrowExceptionInPrivateScript) are out of scope for this analysis.
Cross-realm or cross-context object behavior of the returned getter result is not addressed by the shown code.

verdict.summary: The shown SSH_MSG_KEXDH_INIT packet callback performs no direct memory, bounds, integer, or input-validation operations. It only validates the handshake state, dispatches on kex_type (with a safe default), and forwards the attacker-controlled packet to unshown handler functions. No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability exists within the shown code.

evidence.reason: Sink: unguarded get_bits1() in the SKIP_TYPE_ROW else-branch. The only guard before it (lines 24-26) checks get_bits_left < 1, i.e., just the row-flag bit; the loop at lines 31-33 then consumes mb_width bits from the attacker-controlled GetBitContext s->gb with no check. With the flag bit 0 and fewer than mb_width bits remaining (truncated/attacker-crafted payload), the bit reader advances past the buffer end and, beyond the framework padding, performs a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

Sink: same unguarded get_bits1() pattern transposed in the SKIP_TYPE_COL else-branch. The guard at lines 39-41 covers only the single column-flag bit, then the loop at lines 46-48 makes mb_height unguarded reads. An attacker-set skip_type=3 with column flag 0 and fewer than mb_height bits remaining triggers the same heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: mb_type is allocated with at least mb_stride * mb_height entries and mb_stride >= mb_width (FFmpeg MpegEncContext invariants), so the mb_type[...] stores in all branches are in-bounds; writes are not the vulnerability.
s->mb_width and s->mb_height are positive and originate from picture-header dimensions set before parse_mb_skip() is called.

The bitstream buffer carries AV_INPUT_BUFFER_PADDING_SIZE bytes of readable padding by framework contract, which masks small logical over-reads (e.g., the 2-bit skip_type read at line 6 and single flag reads).
limitations: The physical heap over-read requires the unguarded bit consumption (mb_width or mb_height bits) to exceed the buffer's readable padding; if dimension caps in code not shown bounded mb_width/mb_height below that threshold, only a logical over-read past the stream end occurs. Real-world OSS-Fuzz/FFmpeg reports confirm the physical over-read in this exact function.

The int multiplication s->mb_height * s->mb_width in the SKIP_TYPE_MPEG guard (line 15) could conceptually overflow for extreme dimensions and bypass the guard; whether such dimensions are reachable depends on limit checks outside this snippet - unconfirmed.
The unguarded get_bits(&s->gb, 2) at line 6 can read beyond the logical stream end when fewer than 2 bits remain; with framework padding this is a robustness concern only, not an OOB.
An out-of-bounds mb_type store would require a caller to violate the mb_stride >= mb_width / allocation-size invariants, which is out of scope for the shown code.

verdict.summary: qemu_register_machine contains no attacker-controlled input, no arithmetic or indexing on external data, and no branches or loops; the only deviation from ideal behavior is a one-time, bounded heap leak of the g_strconcat-ed machine name (plus theoretical NULL/duplicate-name robustness concerns that require a caller to violate QEMU's internal registration contract). If a caller ever passed a QEMUMachine with name == NULL, g_strconcat would read from NULL and crash; no shown code path or input can trigger this, so it is recorded as an unconfirmed robustness concern.

No duplicate-name check precedes type_register; registration of two machines sharing a name could abort via QOM's type assertion, but names are build-time identifiers, so this is not attacker-triggerable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in rpmPackageFilesInstall: fdata is allocated with fc elements (line 15) but indexed by fx (line 68) with no fx < fc guard. evidence.reason: Sink: fdata (allocated with fc elements at line 15) is indexed by fx with no fx < fc check. fx is derived from rpmfiNext(fi) where fi is the attacker-controlled archive reader (payload from line 4 via rpmfiNewArchiveReader at line 53). A crafted RPM whose cpio payload has more entries than fc makes fx >= fc pass the >= 0 loop guard, so &fdata[fx] is out of bounds and the loop body writes OOB (CWE-787/CWE-122).

Defines the heap buffer bound: exactly fc struct filedata_s elements (valid indices 0..fc-1). The vulnerable indexing at line 68 can exceed this bound because fc is the header-declared file count while the archive iterator can yield a larger attacker-controlled count.

assumptions: fc = rpmfilesFC(files) reflects the header-declared file count and is bounded by the header field width, so the allocation itself is a fixed fc-element buffer.
Loops 1, 3, and 4 iterate via rpmfilesIter(files, ...) whose indices are internally consistent with fc; only the archive-reader loop (TR_ADDED path) can diverge from fc.
limitations: The precise ability of rpmfiNext (RPMFI_ITER_READ_ARCHIVE) to return fx >= fc depends on the rpmfi library internals, which are not shown here. If those internals clamp iteration to fc, the OOB would not be reachable; the confirmed reachability relies on the attacker-controlled payload being able to drive fx beyond fc.

xcalloc(fc, ...) failure (e.g., an extremely large fc) would return NULL and cause a NULL dereference at line 25/68; treated as an unchecked-allocation robustness concern, not reported as a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability is reachable within the shown code. The only allocation, 'name' (line 3), is passed by pointer via ti.name (line 5) to type_register (line 10) and freed at line 11, but no shown code dereferences it after the free, and m->name comes from trusted internal QEMUMachine descriptors rather than attacker-controlled input. verdict.summary: dbcs_ptr2len reads p[1] when the first byte is a DBCS lead byte (len==2). The function has no length parameter and performs no bounds check, so a caller passing a pointer whose p[1] lies past the allocation could trigger an out-of-bounds read. evidence.reason: The only input is char_u *p with no accompanying length, so the function cannot verify that a second byte exists. When MB_BYTE2LEN(*p) returns 2, the guard reads p[1] unconditionally, which is an out-of-bounds read if the caller passes a pointer where p[1] lies beyond the allocation end. This is gated only on the byte value, not on any bounds invariant enforced in this function. Because the reachable call sites and their buffer guarantees are not shown, the out-of-bounds read is treated as a robustness concern dependent on a caller contract rather than a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: The function is only ever called with a pointer into a NUL-terminated buffer and with p not pointing at the terminating NUL, so p[1] is always within allocated memory (either a real byte or the terminator).
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read of p[1] if a caller passes p such that p[1] is past the allocation boundary; the shown code lacks a length parameter and any bounds check, but no in-scope call path demonstrates this condition, so it remains an unconfirmed hypothesis.

verdict.summary: parse_mb_skip() consumes get_bits1() bits in loops whose trip counts are controlled by attacker-supplied mb_width/mb_height/skip_type without checking get_bits_left() first. evidence.reason: get_bits1(&s->gb) at this sink reads from the attacker-controlled bitstream. The SKIP_TYPE_* constants map to 0–3 so the 2-bit switch is exhaustive.

get_bits1() internals are not shown; the exact physical OOB read occurs when FFmpeg's safe bitstream reader is disabled. With the default safe reader, the primary observed impact is processing past the logical bitstream end (timeout/robustness).
The upstream fixes for this function also address decoder DoS/timeout paths outside the shown code; those are out of scope for a confirmed finding here.

verdict.summary: SetClipboardText's web path executes a JavaScript string built with emscripten_run_script and embeds the caller-provided text unescaped inside a single-quoted literal. The single-quote guard at line 8 removes the only JS string-delimiter that could break out of that literal, so no concrete value passing the guard can inject code. The blacklist approach is fragile and a trailing backslash or newline produces an unterminated-string SyntaxError, but no confirmed, reachable injection or memory-safety flaw is demonstrated in the shown code.

It is only reachable when line 8's guard (strchr(text, '\'') == NULL) holds, i.e. when 'text' contains no single quote. Because the surrounding JS string is single-quoted and the ASCII apostrophe is the only delimiter that can terminate it and enable injection, and the guard removes that character, no value passing the guard can break out and inject code.

This guard is what prevents a confirmed, reachable injection; its coverage is complete for the apostrophe delimiter, though it is a blacklist rather than proper escaping.

'text' is treated as application-supplied; the shown code does not establish that it is genuinely attacker-controlled.

A 'text' value ending in a backslash or containing a newline produces an unterminated-string SyntaxError in the generated JS, breaking clipboard functionality without executing attacker code; an unconfirmed availability concern, not a security vulnerability.

If the embedding application passes genuinely untrusted data to SetClipboardText, the unsafe emscripten_run_script pattern remains a robustness/hardening concern; this depends on out-of-scope caller behavior and was not confirmed here.

verdict.summary: Unsigned 32-bit wraparound in the fsmeta accumulation lets an attacker-controlled f2fs image make the summed metadata-segment count wrap to a small value below total, bypassing sanity_check_ckpt and returning 0 for an inconsistent layout; downstream f2fs mount code may then trust corrupted segment counts.

With segment_count=0xFFFFFFFF, segment_count_ckpt=0xFFFFFFFC, segment_count_sit=4, rsvd_segment_count=100, and the other fields zero, the true sum is 0x100000064 but fsmeta stores 100; that wrapped value passes the guards at lines  ​15 and ​21-22 and accepts the layout at line  ​32.

assumptions: F2FS_RAW_SUPER, F2FS_CKPT, and f2fs_cp_error are trusted framework-internal helpers whose returned pointers/status are valid for the given sbi.
le32_to_cpu on Linux yields a 32-bit unsigned int, so unsigned int arithmetic in this function is 32-bit.
limitations: The concrete memory-corruption/OOB outcome depends on f2fs mount code that is not shown in this excerpt; this analysis confirms the validation bypass and the integer-overflow cause, not a specific downstream out-of-bounds write/read line.
Exploitation in practice also depends on the attacker's ability to supply a crafted f2fs image to a mounting path and on the privilege model of the affected environment.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() uses the unchecked column parameter as an offset into the current line buffer. A negative column, reachable from operator/change editing states, makes `p + col` point before the line buffer and causes mb_head_off() to perform an out-of-bounds read.

With col == -1 the pointer is one byte before the buffer returned by ml_get_curline(), and mb_head_off() then reads around that out-of-range pointer. The shown code contains no `col >= 0` or `col <= line length` check before this sink.

assumptions: colnr_T is signed, so col can be negative.
has_mbyte is true for multibyte encodings such as UTF-8, enabling the vulnerable branch.
ml_get_curline() returns a line buffer whose valid byte offsets are 0 through the line length, inclusive of the NUL terminator.
limitations: The exact user-command path that supplies a negative col (operator endpoint minus one, reproduced upstream with 've=all' and 'cpo+=$') lives in callers outside this excerpt; it is corroborated by upstream patch 9.0.0218 rather than shown here.
An upper-bound case (col beyond the line length) also yields invalid pointer arithmetic, but no shown caller demonstrates it; treated as a hardening concern, not a confirmed finding.
The confirmed impact is a read-only out-of-bounds access; no write primitive or code-execution path is visible.

verdict.summary: write_refcount_block_entries() uses caller-supplied first_index/last_index with no bounds, sign, or ordering validation. On the cache_refcount_updates path, size = (last_index - first_index) << REFCOUNT_SHIFT can overflow/negate and sign-extend into a huge size_t, and bdrv_pwrite reads 'size' bytes from &s->refcount_block_cache[first_index], giving an out-of-bounds heap read (host memory disclosure into the image file) and a crash, reachable from image-controlled refcount data.

evidence.reason: Sink: the buffer pointer &s->refcount_block_cache[first_index] is formed from the unvalidated int first_index (line 2) and 'size' (line 11) is the unchecked byte count. With cache_refcount_updates true (line 7) and no guard bounding first_index to [0, s->refcount_block_size) or first_index <= last_index, a caller-supplied first_index < 0, first_index >= s->refcount_block_size, or a huge size from line 11 causes bdrp_pwrite to read out of bounds of the heap cache and write those bytes to the backing file (CWE-125).

Enabling flaw: last_index + REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR is signed int addition that overflows for last_index > INT_MAX - REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR, and (last_index - first_index) << REFCOUNT_SHIFT becomes negative when last_index < first_index or wraps when the shift overflows the 32-bit int. The negative int is then assigned to size_t, sign-extending into a huge transfer size that amplifies the out-of-bounds read at line 15 (CWE-190, independently confirmed).

assumptions: cache_refcount_updates is a driver-global flag that can be true (it is the default path for refcount cache updates in QEMU); the analyzed path is its true branch.

s->refcount_block_cache is a heap array of s->refcount_block_size entries, each 1 << REFCOUNT_SHIFT bytes, so valid indices are [0, s->refcount_block_size); this bound is not declared in the shown excerpt.
REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR is a power of two, so the masks at lines 8-10 only align to sector boundaries and never change sign or bound magnitude.
In the enclosing qcow2 driver, first_index/last_index are derived from image-controlled refcount data (e.g., update_refcount() computing indices from offsets/refcounts read from the image file).
limitations: The callers of write_refcount_block_entries() are not shown; the concrete out-of-range index value must be produced by the unshown caller path. If a caller strictly guaranteed 0 <= first_index <= last_index < s->refcount_block_size with no signed overflow, the shown body would be safe; the shown code itself contains no such enforcement.
Signed integer overflow at lines 9 and 11 is undefined behavior in C; the huge-size behavior is the de-facto wrap on two's-complement compilers, so the exact size value is compiler-dependent.

Exploitation requires the attacker to supply a malicious qcow2 image and the cache_refcount_updates path; impact is assessed as out-of-bounds read (host-memory disclosure into the image file and crash), not arbitrary code execution.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only memory access beyond *p is the p[1] read in the condition at line 10, which is reachable only when *p != NUL (early return at lines 5-6). The p[1] == NUL branch (line 11) additionally clamps the returned length to 1 for a trailing DBCS lead byte, preventing callers from treating the terminator as character data. A one-byte out-of-bounds read would require a caller to pass a non-NUL-terminated buffer whose final byte is a lead byte, which violates the caller contract and is not reachable from the shown code.

evidence.reason: This guard excludes the only input state in which p[1] could fall outside the allocation: an empty string whose sole allocated byte is the terminator. After this guard, *p is a non-NUL byte, so in any NUL-terminated buffer p[1] is at minimum the in-bounds terminator.

The only access beyond *p. It executes only when *p != NUL (lines 5-6) and MB_BYTE2LEN(*p) returned 2 (line 9); p[1] then reads either a real second byte or the in-bounds terminator, so the constant index 1 cannot exceed the allocation for a NUL-terminated input.

assumptions: p points into a NUL-terminated byte buffer with storage for the terminator, as guaranteed by Vim's internal string contracts (for example, line text from ml_get() and scratch buffers).
For DBCS encodings, MB_BYTE2LEN(x) returns only 1 or 2 and is a lookup/range test indexed by the byte value 0..255, so the macro call itself cannot go out of bounds for any *p.
char_u is an unsigned character type, so no sign-extension affects *p when used as a table index or comparison operand.
limitations: If a caller passed a non-NUL-terminated buffer whose last byte is a DBCS lead byte, the p[1] read on line 10 would read one byte past the allocation (CWE-125). This requires an out-of-scope caller violating the NUL-termination contract and is not reachable through any path in the shown code, so it is recorded as an unconfirmed robustness concern, not a vulnerability.
The function exposes no length parameter and cannot itself prove that p[1] is within the allocation; that proof is delegated to the NUL-termination invariant the shown code relies on.
Returning length 2 for a lead byte followed by a non-lead byte is encoding-semantics behavior and a potential misparse, but it is not a memory-safety failure within this function.

verdict.summary: In SProcXkbSelectEvents, dataLeft is unsigned and its accounting is inconsistent for size==1 notify types: the bounds check at the guard uses size==1 (requires only 2 bytes) but line 67 subtracts (size*2)=4. With dataLeft==2 this subtract underflows to 0xFFFFFFFE, which defeats the guard for subsequent iterations, so the following swaps(&from.c16[0])/swapl(&from.c32[0]) reads out of bounds past the request buffer, enabling memory disclosure and a crash.

evidence.reason: dataLeft (line 20, unsigned) is attacker-influenced via stuff->length (line 23) and the loop size via stuff->affectWhich (line 24). For a size==1 notify type (Bell/ActionMessage/CompatMap), the guard only checks dataLeft>=2, but the else branch sets size=2 and line 67 subtracts 4. With dataLeft==2, 2-4 underflows to 0xFFFFFFFE. verdict.summary: Unsigned 32-bit integer overflow in the fsmeta accumulation lets attacker-controlled on-disk segment counts wrap modulo 2^32, so the fsmeta >= total and F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS sanity gates are bypassed and a corrupted checkpoint layout is accepted as valid, failing open the mount-time validation gate that guards later segment-accounting/geometry code.

evidence.reason: fsmeta is a 32-bit unsigned int (line 3); five attacker-controlled le32 values from the on-disk superblock/checkpoint are summed without any bound or widening cast, so unsigned addition wraps modulo 2^32. Example: segment_count_ckpt=0xFFFFFFFF, segment_count_sit=0x1000, rsvd_segment_count=1 yields fsmeta=0x1000 (4096) while the true sum exceeds 2^32.

The guard compares the wrapped fsmeta against total=segment_count. With total=5000 and wrapped fsmeta=4096, the not-taken branch is reached, the image passes the < total and >= F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS checks, and the function returns 0 despite the real metadata segment sum far exceeding total, defeating the validation the gate is meant to enforce.

assumptions: The on-disk f2fs_checkpoint arrays cur_node_segno/cur_node_blkoff/cur_data_segno/cur_data_blkoff are declared with exactly NR_CURSEG_NODE_TYPE and NR_CURSEG_DATA_TYPE entries (standard f2fs layout), so the loop indices at lines 33-42 are always in-bounds.
sbi->blocks_per_seg is a trusted kernel invariant (512 for 4 KiB blocks) and is not directly attacker-controllable inside this function.
F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS is a small positive constant (e.g., 9), so a wrapped fsmeta can satisfy fsmeta >= F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS.
This function runs on the mount path before the filesystem structures are used, which is how a crafted image reaches it.
limitations: The concrete out-of-bounds read/write sink that the bypassed gate would have prevented lives in mount/segment-accounting code not shown here; the exact corruption primitive and offsets are not confirmed from this snippet.
Consistency between segment_count_main and segment_count/fsmeta is not validated in the shown code; any resulting issue depends on code outside this function.
End-to-end impact assumes a local attacker can mount a crafted filesystem image; the reachability of exploitation beyond the failed-open gate is not verifiable within the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability in ssh_packet_kexdh_init: rc is assigned on every switch path before the rc == SSH_ERROR test (lines 14/18/23/28 vs line 30), the wrong-state goto (line 9) jumps past that test to the error label (line 32), and the function performs no buffer, length, or index arithmetic on the attacker-controlled packet. All packet parsing occurs in out-of-scope handler functions.

evidence.reason: State gate: out-of-order KEXDH_INIT packets are rejected and jump to the error label; because the label (line 32) sits below the rc==SSH_ERROR test (line 30), this taken branch never reads rc, so no uninitialized-value read exists.

Every possible kex_type value reaches an arm that assigns rc before break (lines 14, 18, 23) or the default arm which assigns rc = SSH_ERROR (line 28), so line 30 always sees an initialized rc; unknown kex types degrade to a clean SSH_ERROR, not undefined behavior.

Error handling: a failed kex handler only flips the session state enum to SSH_SESSION_STATE_ERROR, and the function always returns SSH_PACKET_USED; the attacker-controlled packet is consumed without any buffer operation in this function.

assumptions: The packet dispatch layer invokes this callback only with a live session object and holds the session lock, making session a valid non-NULL pointer.
session->next_crypto is allocated by the session kex setup before SSH_MSG_KEXDH_INIT can be dispatched; the line-7 DH_STATE_INIT gate enforces the corresponding sequencing.
SSH_ERROR, SSH_OK, and the session/handshake state enumerations are framework-defined constants compared by value, with no arithmetic that could overflow.
limitations: Attacker-controlled parsing of `packet` happens inside ssh_server_kexdh_init / ssh_server_ecdh_init / ssh_server_curve25519_init, whose code is not shown; any memory-safety defects there cannot be confirmed by this analysis and would need separate review.
NULL dereference of session->next_crypto would require an out-of-scope caller to violate the session/kex lifecycle invariant, so it is recorded as a robustness concern, not a vulnerability.

A crafted stream of repeated KEXDH_INIT packets is not a memory-safety issue here: wrong-state packets are rejected by the gate and any handler failure sets SSH_SESSION_STATE_ERROR, which the session loop is responsible for terminating.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability. The only guest-controlled indices are field-bounded (SR is 4 bits, 0..15; rS is 5 bits, 0..31), the privilege check CHK_SV precedes the helper call, and the helper-side stores are bounds-checked.

evidence.reason: The only guest-controlled indices reaching the helper are SR(...) (masked to 0..15) and rS(...) (masked to 0..31), both strictly within cpu_gpr[32] and env->sr/ppc_store_slb bounds; CHK_SV on line 7 already blocked user-mode execution before this sink is emitted.

assumptions: SR(ctx->opcode) extracts a 4-bit field (range 0..15) and rS(ctx->opcode) extracts a 5-bit field (range 0..31), as defined in the QEMU PowerPC decoder.
cpu_gpr has 32 entries and env->sr has at least 16 entries.
CHK_SV correctly reflects the guest privilege state via the translation context.
limitations: If SR were redefined to a wider field, or env->sr were smaller than 16 entries, an out-of-bounds write could become reachable; the shown code alone does not demonstrate that.
The 64-bit helper path ignores ppc_store_slb's return value, but ppc_store_slb performs its own slot check, so this is a correctness concern, not a confirmed memory-safety issue.
Any bypass of CHK_SV would depend on stale ctx->pr state maintained outside this function and is out of scope.

verdict.summary: write_refcount_block_entries trusts the caller-supplied refcount-block indices: the only guard (first_index >= 0 at lines 10-12) leaves last_index and the index range entirely unchecked. A crafted-image-driven parameter pair with last_index < first_index (e.g., first_index=512, last_index=100) makes (last_index - first_index) negative at line 16, which converts to a size_t of ~2^64-512 and drives bdrv_pwrite (lines 18-20) to read that many bytes from the cluster-sized refcount_block_cache, producing a heap out-of-bounds read: host QEMU crash/DoS and host-heap disclosure written into the image file.

evidence.reason: This is the only validation applied to the attacker-influenced parameters first_index/last_index (lines 1-2). It covers only first_index < 0; it does not bound either index against the refcount block entry count (cluster_size >> REFCOUNT_SHIFT) and does not check last_index >= first_index, so the dangerous operations below remain reachable.

For first_index=512, last_index=100 (both pass the line 10 guard), the alignment at lines 13-15 yields first_index=512 and last_index=256, so the int difference is -256 and (with REFCOUNT_SHIFT=1) the value stored into the 64-bit size_t is 2^64-512 (integer underflow, CWE-191), rather than a small byte count.

The sink: bdrv_pwrite reads size bytes from &s->refcount_block_cache[first_index], a heap buffer of cluster_size (e.g., 65536) bytes. With size = 2^64-512 the read is out of bounds immediately (CWE-125); independently, first_index=40000 (>32768 entries for a 64 KiB cluster) makes the source pointer itself out of bounds. Over-read bytes are written into the host image file at refcount_block_offset + (first_index << REFCOUNT_SHIFT), giving heap disclosure and crash/DoS.

assumptions: REFCOUNT_SHIFT=1 (2-byte refcount entries) and REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR=256 (512-byte sectors) as defined in the QEMU qcow2 header, not shown in the snippet.
s->refcount_block_cache is allocated as cluster_size bytes in qcow2_open, so in-bounds entry indices are [0, cluster_size >> REFCOUNT_SHIFT).
int is 32-bit and size_t is 64-bit on the host build.
The reaching path requires cache_refcount_updates == 0, otherwise lines 7-9 return before the sink.
limitations: The callers (e.g., update_refcount) are not shown, so the full attacker-to-parameter trace is not visible inside this unit; if callers always pass ordered, in-block indices, the flaw is a defense-in-depth gap rather than an externally reachable bug. The historic crafted-image qcow2 exploits support treating it as reachable, hence the promoted verdict with reduced confidence.
Signed left shifts at lines 14 and 16 are undefined behavior in C; the exact wrapped values (e.g., -512) assume common two's-complement behavior on the host compiler.
Overflow of last_index + REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR at line 14 requires last_index >= INT_MAX-255 and its effect is compiler-dependent; kept as a robustness concern, not a separate confirmed finding.

bdrv_pwrite's handling of an oversized length (short writes, clamping, failure) is not shown; the source-buffer over-read at line 20 occurs regardless because size already exceeds the remaining cache bytes.

verdict.summary: mov_read_stsz reads an attacker-controlled 32-bit sample count (entries) from the container byte stream with no validation and uses it to size av_malloc(entries * sizeof(long)) and to bound the sample_sizes fill loop. On 32-bit targets the size_t product wraps for values such as 0x40000001, yielding a 4-byte allocation while the loop writes ~2^30 entries, causing a heap out-of-bounds write; on all targets the same path enables multi-GiB allocations and ~2^31-iteration loops (resource exhaustion).

evidence.reason: Taint source: get_be32 returns an attacker-controlled 32-bit unsigned value from pb and narrows it into a signed int with no range check; this value later sizes the heap allocation (line 17) and bounds the write loop (line 20).

The only guard checks sc->sample_size (set to 0 by the attacker at line 9), so entries flows unvalidated into entries * sizeof(long). With entries = 0x40000001 on a 32-bit build the size_t product wraps to 4 bytes, allocating room for 1 long while the loop writes 2^30 entries.

Out-of-bounds write sink: the loop writes entries long-sized values; combined with the line 17 wrap the largest reachable index (entries-1 = 0x40000000) exceeds the 1-element allocation, corrupting the heap (CWE-787). Even without wraparound, entries = 0x7FFFFFFF forces a ~16 GiB allocation and a 2^31-iteration loop (resource exhaustion).

assumptions: The heap-overflow impact assumes a 32-bit build where sizeof(long) == 4 and size_t is 32 bits, so entries * sizeof(long) wraps for values >= 2^30.
The zero/small wrapped allocation is assumed to succeed (glibc-style malloc(0)/malloc(4) returning a usable non-NULL pointer) so the fill loop executes.
get_be32 is assumed to return 0 at EOF without itself reading out of bounds (ByteIOContext internals are not shown).
The demuxer is assumed to invoke this atom callback only with nb_streams >= 1, making the line 3 stream indexing safe by caller contract.
limitations: On 64-bit LP64 targets entries * sizeof(long) cannot wrap because entries is bounded by INT_MAX; only the multi-GiB allocation and 2^31-iteration DoS (CWE-400-class) apply there, not the confirmed out-of-bounds write.
Whether av_malloc of ~16 GiB fails cleanly (line 19 -1) or succeeds depends on the allocator and overcommit settings; the failure path is a clean parse error.
A potential out-of-bounds read inside get_be32 at EOF depends on ByteIOContext internals not shown and was not evaluated as a separate finding.
c->fc->streams[c->fc->nb_streams-1] is unvalidated if nb_streams == 0; reachability depends on an out-of-scope caller contract and is not counted as a confirmed vulnerability.
sc->sample_count may exceed the number of samples actually present in the file; downstream use of sample_sizes by other parsing code is outside the shown code and not evaluated.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. The guard on entries (line 11) bounds entries below floor(UINT_MAX/sizeof(long)), which makes the av_malloc size arithmetic (line 19) overflow-free on both 32-bit and 64-bit platforms, the allocation failure is checked (line 20), and the loop index (lines 22-23) stays within the allocated array.

The allocation at line 19 reserves entries long slots. The loop condition i < entries bounds the maximum index to entries-1, which is strictly less than the number of slots, so every write to sc->sample_sizes[i] is in-bounds; the loop terminates because entries is finite.

Attacker-controlled entries (up to ~2^29 on LP64) can force a large allocation and a long read loop, a resource-exhaustion robustness concern; av_malloc failure is handled, so no memory-safety impact is confirmed.

Downstream consumers of sc->sample_count / sc->sample_sizes (e.g., sample table iteration in unshown code) are out of scope and not evaluated here.

verdict.summary: The calloc implementation guards the n*lb multiplication with `if (lb && n > SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;`, which is the standard, correct overflow check. For every input class (lb==0, n==0, both nonzero) the product n*lb cannot exceed SIZE_MAX, so the allocations at the return paths are never reached with an overflowing size. No reachable integer-overflow or memory-safety vulnerability is present in the shown code.

evidence.snippet:
if (lb && n > SIZE_MAX / lb)
      return NULL;
evidence.reason: This is the only guard on the later `n*lb` multiplication. When lb is nonzero, it returns NULL exactly when n*lb would exceed SIZE_MAX; when lb or n is zero the product is 0, which cannot overflow. Therefore the multiplication at the allocation sinks is never computed with an overflowing value, so the integer-overflow candidate fails reachability.

assumptions: SIZE_MAX is the maximum value of size_t, and both n and lb are size_t so the multiplication and division are performed in size_t width.
REDIRECT_MALLOC and GC_malloc_uncollectable correctly handle the byte count passed to them and do not themselves truncate the size.
limitations: A caller passing extremely large but non-overflowing n*lb could trigger a large or failed allocation, but this is a resource/robustness concern, not an integer-safety or memory-safety vulnerability, and no such attacker path is demonstrated in the shown code.

The caller-address range checks and GC_lib_bounds logic rely on framework invariants not shown here; a mismatch could route an allocation to uncollectable memory, but that is an internal correctness concern outside the demonstrated attack surface.

If formatting removes lines and a stale Visual-mode line number is smaller than the deleted count, the addition wraps to 0/ULONG_MAX, corrupting window redraw state and potentially causing out-of-bounds redraw access.

limitations: The exact redraw routine that consumes w_old_cursor_lnum/w_old_visual_lnum is not in the supplied fragment, so the concrete out-of-bounds memory sink is not directly shown; the OOB consequence is inferred from the corrupted line-number state.
u_save range arithmetic,and other caller-provided invariants, cannot be verified from the fragment alone.

verdict.summary: The calloc implementation safely guards the n*lb multiplication with the canonical overflow check `if (lb && n > GC_SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;`. Because the guard is evaluated before both allocation sinks (GC_malloc_uncollectable(n*lb) and REDIRECT_MALLOC(n*lb)), no integer overflow is reachable, so no vulnerability is confirmed.

if (lb && n > GC_SIZE_MAX / lb)
      return NULL;

assumptions: GC_SIZE_MAX is defined as the maximum size_t value for the target platform (required for compilation).

limitations: The static GC_bool lib_bounds_set flag (line 9) is accessed without synchronization, allowing a benign data race where GC_init_lib_bounds() might run more than once; this is a defensive-hardening/robustness concern with no attacker-controlled path or confirmed security impact in the shown code.

verdict.summary: After the D-Bus auth handshake, the proxy allocates a buffer of attacker-controlled size: g_dbus_message_bytes_needed() returns total message length derived from the message header's body-length field, and the only guard is a negative check. The attacker can choose a body length near the 32-bit maximum, so the branch at line 76 (full header read) leads directly to `buffer_new(required, buffer)` at line 89, triggering an uncontrolled multi-gigabyte allocation and a denial-of-service condition. An attacker who completes the D-Bus auth handshake can reach this path via `client->authenticated = TRUE` (line 69) and the `buffer->pos == buffer->size` branch (line 76).

assumptions: buffer_read() never writes more data into a Buffer than its allocated capacity, so the 1-byte and 64-byte auth reads are memory-safe.
g_dbus_message_bytes_needed() returns a length based on the D-Bus header, including attacker-controlled body length; no hidden size cap is assumed in the shown code.
side->header_buffer is a full-capacity buffer whose data pointer is valid for at least buffer->size bytes.

An out-of-bounds read from `g_bytes_new (buffer->data + buffer->size,: extra_data)` would depend on find_auth_end() returning auth_end > buffer->pos; that contract is not shown, so it remains an unconfirmed hypothesis.
Leaked/overwritten side->extra_input_data references are a memory-management robustness concern but not confirmed as an attacker-triggerable integrity/availability flaw in the shown scope.
The g_malloc abort on failed allocation is the consequence of the unbounded allocation finding, not an independent vulnerability.

verdict.summary: No confirmed, reachable vulnerability in the shown code. Attacker-controlled flags and per-item lengths are bounded by the 16-bit loop limits and the len/maxCutText guards: the caps branch checks len >= 4 + 4*num before reading num values into the 16-element array, and the provide branch allocates each buffer exactly at lengths[num] only after confirming lengths[num] <= maxCutText. Remaining concerns (uninitialized tail entries of the length/buffer arrays, allocation/stream-exhaustion denial of service, and the (size_t)maxCutText cast if that config could be negative) depend on out-of-scope handler contracts or trusted configuration and are recorded as limitations.

num counts only the 16 low bits of attacker-controlled flags (max 16), and the guard len < 4 + 4*num (max 68, no integer overflow for size_t num <= 16) ensures the second loop can read exactly num U32s. Largest write index is num-1 <= 15, inside lengths[16]; an all-16-bits-set flags value requires len >= 68 or an exception is thrown, so no out-of-bounds access is reachable.

num advances only for accepted items (max 16 set bits -> indices 0..15 within lengths[16]/buffers[16]), and allocation/copy occur only when attacker-controlled lengths[num] <= (size_t)maxCutText, so each heap buffer is exactly sized and readBytes writes at most lengths[num] bytes. verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled JPEG2000 header fields flow unchecked into jpc_pi_nextrpcl: signed-overflow in precinct/step arithmetic can produce invalid prcno values used as heap indices into prclyrnos (OOB read/write or assertion abort), and zero xstep/ystep/rpx divisors cause SIGFPE/DoS.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled packet/slice sizes are multiplied by 8 in signed 32-bit arithmetic with no range check, and are used to initialize/extend the GetBitContext. limitations: The precise out-of-bounds memory access occurs inside rv10_decode_picture_header/rv20_decode_picture_header and ff_h263_decode_mb, whose bodies are not shown here; the reachable tainted path is shown, but the exact dereference is inferred from standard FFmpeg GetBitContext semantics.

A practical exploit needs the calling layer to permit a slice size of roughly >=256 MB or a negative size; this is consistent with the historical FFmpeg RV10 slice-parsing flaws but depends partly on caller behavior not included in the snippet.

The mb_width*mb_height / mb_y*mb_width products at lines 20–21 canalso wrap if dimension-validation invariants outside this function are violated, which could defeat the mb_count > left guard; unconfirmed here, so not counted as a separate finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed attacker-triggerable vulnerability in the shown code. ctx->alg_decrypt(ctx->ctx_decrypt ? ctx->ctx_decrypt : ctx->ctx_encrypt,

evidence.reason: ECB decrypt sink: reads len bytes from in and writes exactly len bytes to out. verdict.summary: hash_passwords replaces the intended random salt (RAND_bytes is commented out) with an unconditional all-zero 32-byte salt via memset(...,0,32). Every user therefore gets the identical predictable salt, so equal passwords produce equal PBKDF2 hashes, enabling cross-user hash correlation and making offline/precomputed cracking of one user transferable to all users.

evidence.reason: The only salt-generation call (RAND_bytes, line 27) is dead code, and the unconditional memset at line 31, executed for every i in [0, count) of the loop at line 25, sets the 32-byte salt to the constant all-zero value. The salt is thus identical and fully predictable for every user and every run, which is the taint source feeding the vulnerable sink.

Attacker-supplied password (passwords[i] from argv via line 59) flows directly into the password-derivation sink, with the salt argument taken from the buffer that line 31 zeroed. Because the sink is reached on every loop iteration with the same zero salt, identical passwords produce identical hashes, confirming CWE-760 reachability and impact.

assumptions: In main, usernames.size() == passwords.size() == count by construction (lines 53-54), so hash_passwords' indexing of passwords[i] is in-bounds for the shown entrypoint (line 62).
argv has exactly argc entries (indices 0..argc-1), and the OS forbids NUL bytes and 2 GiB strings in argv, making the length() narrowing and index arithmetic safe in this flow.
PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 10000 iterations is treated as the intended KDF; the finding concerns only the salt.

Implicit size_t to int conversion of passwords[i].length() (line 34) could pass a wrong/negative length for passwords >= 2 GiB; only theoretical because argv is bounded by ARG_MAX.
An even argc leaves one trailing username silently unused (e.g., argc=4 ignores argv[3]); this is a behavioral quirk, not a memory error.
The usernames parameter is unused; any intended per-user salt derivation from usernames is absent, which compounds but does not independently change the salt finding.

verdict.summary: avc_mp4_find_startcode never validates that nal_length_size is positive or within the 1..4 range assumed for MP4 length prefixes.
